title: FOOD SUPPLEMENTS – friend or foe?
subtitle: For questions 1–8, read the text and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap. There is an example at the beginning (0).
passage:
A fast growing and immensely profitable industry in many countries, there are [[0]] of dietary supplements on the market, with individuals taking them whether they are feeling out of [[1]] or simply aiming to stay on form. However, whether they have any true efficacy is another matter entirely.

For many current researchers, the jury doesn't seem to be just out, it has come back with quite a [[2]] verdict that there are almost no tangible benefits to [[3]] on such supplements. Firstly, they cite that nutritional [[4]] don't necessarily need to be addressed by supplements, since such a wide variety of food products, especially in countries like the US, are [[5]] with vitamins and minerals to ensure a balanced diet. Additionally, these supplements aren't [[6]] to the same manufacturing standards as medicines, meaning that some of the more unscrupulous supplement providers can oversell the health benefits without providing a [[7]] of evidence. So, perhaps the lesson for us all here is that when it comes to health you just can't [[8]] a balanced, varied diet.

items.explainCorrect: Fixed phrase **out of sorts** = not feeling quite right / slightly unwell.

explainIfChosen.0: **Out of mend** is not an idiom.
explainIfChosen.2: **Out of touch** means disconnected — wrong meaning here.
explainIfChosen.3: **Out of elements** is not standard English.

items.explainCorrect: A **damning verdict** strongly condemns something — fits researchers' negative conclusion.

explainIfChosen.0: **Malicious** describes intent to harm — odd for a jury's verdict.
explainIfChosen.1: **Elusive** means hard to catch — does not collocate with *verdict*.
explainIfChosen.2: **Fatal** suggests death — too extreme for this context.

items.explainCorrect: **Fork out on** (BrE) = spend money on — natural before *supplements*.

explainIfChosen.1: **Press on** means continue despite difficulty — wrong verb.
explainIfChosen.2: **Chip in** means contribute jointly — not paying for your own pills.
explainIfChosen.3: **Bounce back** means recover — wrong collocation after *benefits to*.

items.explainCorrect: **Nutritional deficiencies** = lack of essential nutrients — standard collocation.

explainIfChosen.0: **Infractions** are rule violations — wrong semantic field.
explainIfChosen.2: **Inadequacies** is vaguer; *nutritional deficiencies* is the set phrase.
explainIfChosen.3: **Shortages** suggest supply problems, not lack in the body.

items.explainCorrect: Foods **fortified with** vitamins/minerals = nutrients added during processing.

explainIfChosen.0: **Embodied with** is not used for food enrichment.
explainIfChosen.1: **Doctored** suggests tampering or falsifying — negative tone.
explainIfChosen.3: **Garnished** means decorated on top — not bulk nutrient addition.

items.explainCorrect: **Held to standards** = required to meet the same rules as medicines.

explainIfChosen.2: **Pinned to** does not work with manufacturing rules.
explainIfChosen.3: **Drawn to standards** is not a collocation.

items.explainCorrect: Idiom **not a shred of evidence** = absolutely no proof at all.

explainIfChosen.0: **Strip of evidence** is not the fixed phrase.
explainIfChosen.3: **Shave of evidence** is not a collocation.

items.explainCorrect: Idiom **you can't beat a balanced diet** = nothing is better than eating well.

explainIfChosen.1: **Strike a diet** confuses with *strike a balance*.
explainIfChosen.2: **Crush a diet** suggests destroying it — wrong meaning.
